beats: A ship drifted empty across the Atlantic, with its lifeboat gone.
This is the Mary Celeste, 1872. Ten people, including a two-year-old girl, simply gone.
No fight. Their belongings untouched. Six months of food still on board.
Only one thing was missing: the lifeboat. They left in a hurry.
Toxic fumes? A waterspout? A panic that turned deadly? No one knows.
Not one of them was ever seen again. Weeks later, their empty ship was still out there, because
Nine hikers fled their tent barefoot into a frozen night.
Russia, 1959. Minus twenty-five degrees. Some were found a kilometre away, without shoes.
Some had crushed skulls and ribs, but almost no outside wounds.
People blamed avalanches, secret weapons, even something unexplained.
In 2021, scientists said a small slab avalanche could explain the injuries.
But nine experts, fleeing into certain death? What scared them so much that
Over one hundred colonists vanished, leaving one carved word.
Roanoke, 1587. Their governor sailed to England for supplies, leaving his newborn granddaughter behind.
War trapped him there for three years.
When he returned, the settlement was empty. No bodies. No graves.
Just one word on a post: Croatoan, the name of a nearby island.
A storm stopped him from ever searching it. To this day, nobody knows why
A six-hundred-year-old book still has no readable language.
The Voynich Manuscript. Two hundred and forty pages in a script that matches no known language.
Plants that do not exist. Strange star maps. Tiny bathing figures.
Carbon dating proves it is from the early fourteen hundreds. Not a modern fake.
The best codebreakers of both world wars tried. Every one of them failed.
A lost language, or a brilliant hoax? It sits at Yale today, because
Three lighthouse keepers vanished; one coat stayed behind.
Scotland, December 1900. The Flannan Isles light went dark.
Inside, the lamp was clean. Beds made. Nothing out of place.
Outside, iron railings were twisted, equipment ripped away by the sea.
A giant wave, they said. But why were all three outside at once, in winter?
No bodies were ever found. And the strangest clue of all is still this:
A dead man had no labels, no name, and a secret code.
Adelaide, 1948. No wallet. No name. No cause of death.
In a hidden pocket, two words: Tamam Shud. It means, it is ended.
They were torn from a book of Persian poetry. Inside that book, a code nobody has cracked.
In 2022, DNA suggested his name was Carl Webb.
But who killed him, and what does the code say? It all began when
Something exploded over Siberia, a thousand times Hiroshima, and left no crater.
June 1908. Eighty million trees flattened in an instant.
People sixty kilometres away were thrown off their feet. The night sky glowed over Europe.
Scientists arrived years later expecting a giant meteorite. They found nothing.
Most think a space rock burst in the air, kilometres above the ground.
Over a city, it would have erased it. Could it happen again? Remember,
Divers found a computer in a shipwreck, and it was two thousand years old.
X-rays revealed more than thirty precise bronze gears hidden inside the rock.
Turn its handle, and it predicted eclipses, moon phases, even the Olympic Games.
Nothing this complex appears again for over a thousand years.
Who built it? And how was that knowledge simply lost?
We only know because, in 1901,
A man hijacked a plane, jumped into the night with the cash, and vanished.
1971. He called himself Dan Cooper, and calmly handed a flight attendant a note: I have a bomb.
He demanded two hundred thousand dollars and four parachutes.
Over the forests of Washington, he opened the rear stairs and leapt into the rain.
Years later, a boy found some of the cash buried by a river.
Did he die, or get away with it? The FBI still can't say, because
Five Navy bombers vanished, then the plane sent to find them vanished too.
December 1945, off Florida. How did fourteen airmen and a rescue plane disappear?
His compasses failed, the leader radioed, and he thought he was over the Florida Keys.
But they were likely near the Bahamas, so his corrections led them farther out to sea.
Proven: five bombers and a rescue plane were lost. Probable: the bombers ditched, out of fuel. Unknown: where they sank.
The Triangle got the legend; the evidence points to a wrong guess over a winter sea.
A boat carrying twenty-five people was found drifting, and everyone was gone.
1955. The Joyita left Samoa for a two day trip to Tokelau.
She never arrived. Five weeks later, she was found far off course.
Half sunk. Cargo missing. Life rafts gone.
Her radio was set to the distress frequency.
No bodies were ever found. Nobody knows what happened, but
A city prescribed more dancing for people who could not stop.
Within weeks, dozens of people in Strasbourg joined her, dancing until they collapsed.
The city's leaders thought more dancing would cure them, so they hired musicians and built a stage.
It only made things worse. Some accounts say up to four hundred people were affected.
Historians still argue over the cause: poisoned bread, or mass panic after years of hunger.
What could make hundreds of people dance until they dropped?
Two men died on a hill wearing lead eye masks.
August 1966, near Rio. No wounds, and doctors found no cause of death.
Next to them, police found a notebook with strange instructions.
Swallow the capsules at six thirty. Protect metals. Wait for the mask signal.
That same evening, a woman nearby saw a glowing orange object over the hill.
What signal were they waiting for? Nobody has ever found out.
A boat ran empty, with food on the table and no crew.
Australia, 2007. Three men set off on a fishing trip along the Great Barrier Reef.
Days later, their boat, the Kaz II, was found drifting with the laptop still running.
The life jackets were still on board, and the radio worked fine.
Investigators believe they fell overboard, one after another. But all three?
Their bodies were never found. What really happened out there?
A killer mailed codes, but police never learned his name.
California, late 1960s. A killer who called himself the Zodiac began writing to newspapers.
He was linked to at least five murders, and he wanted everyone to know.
One of his codes stayed unsolved for fifty-one years, until amateur codebreakers cracked it in 2020.
But the message did not reveal his name. Thousands were suspected, and no one was ever charged.
His identity is still unknown. Who was the Zodiac?
Giant desert animals seem designed for eyes in the sky.
In Peru, about two thousand years ago, the Nazca people scraped these lines into the desert.
There is a hummingbird, a monkey and a spider. Some are bigger than a football field.
They have survived for centuries because it almost never rains there.
Recently, researchers found hundreds more hidden figures.
But why make drawings that you can only see from the sky?
Dinner waited on a grounded ship, but its crew was gone.
January 1921. Off Cape Hatteras, the Carroll A. Deering ran onto the sandbanks.
Rescuers found food ready in the galley, but all eleven men were gone.
The lifeboats were missing, and so were the captain's papers.
People blamed pirates, a mutiny, even the Bermuda Triangle.
None of the crew was ever found. What happened on board?
A burned body had eight names, but no confirmed identity.
Norway, 1970. Hikers found a woman's body in a remote valley near Bergen.
Every label had been cut from her clothes, so no one could trace them.
At the station, police found her suitcases, with wigs and notes in code.
She had travelled across Europe using at least eight false names.
Was she a spy, a smuggler, or a witness? Fifty years later, no one knows.
A prospector claimed a gold mountain, then took its location to his grave.
Arizona's Superstition Mountains. A German miner known as the Dutchman claimed he had a secret mine there.
Before he died in 1891, he supposedly described where it was.
Since then, thousands of people have searched the mountains.
Some of them never came back.
The gold has never been found. Did it ever exist?
An island had writing, then lost everyone who could read it.
Easter Island. In the 1860s, missionaries found wooden tablets covered in tiny glyphs.
But slave raids and disease had nearly wiped out the island's people.
When outsiders asked, no one left could clearly read the tablets.
Only about two dozen survive today, in museums around the world.
Is it a real lost language? No one has ever been able to read it.
A British lord vanished after a murder, leaving no body.
London, 1974. The family nanny was killed at the home of Lord Lucan's wife.
An inquest later named Lord Lucan as the killer.
His borrowed car was found near the coast, at Newhaven.
For decades, people reported seeing him around the world.
He was declared dead in 2016. Where did he go?
